meta.title: The Warning in the Kitchen
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer uses absolute words to raise the stakes.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 115w at FK 7.4, part_2 109w at FK 5.6, part_3 104w at FK 6.5. The load is absolute wording: 'no use for jam', 'great care', and 'must not burn'.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Isabella Beeton, The Book of Household Management (1861), under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Beeton, Isabella. The Book of Household Management. 1861. Project Gutenberg eBook #10136, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10136, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: The authoring pass split long sentences, simplified rare words, and restored the source's warning as an instruction; no facts added.
source.survey: A household manual explains why fruit is preserved and how it should be picked and stored, then how long boiling thickens the syrup, and ends with a sharp caution about the fire.
source.drafted_by: LessonBot harness (DeepSeek 1017), adapted from the human source; source review completed

session.difficulty_basis: absolute wording: 'no use for jam', 'great care', 'must not burn'

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: Fruit is a key item for health. The food lover can hardly have any treats without it. So, since it is so valuable, when we cannot have it fresh, we must keep it. It has long been a goal to keep fruit by some cheap method, but by one that would still keep it fit for cooking uses, like making tarts and other similar dishes. The cost of keeping them with sugar is a serious problem; for, unless the sugar is used in large amounts, success is very uncertain. Sugar is also too strong for and destroys the slightly sour taste so wanted in many fruits: those kept this way are mainly meant for dessert.
passage.part_2: Fruit you plan to keep should be gathered in the morning, in dry weather, with the morning sun on it if possible. It will then have its fullest flavour and stay good longer than fruit gathered at any other time. Until fruit can be used, put it in the dairy, an ice-house, or the fridge. In an icehouse it will remain fresh and plump for several days. Fruit gathered in wet or foggy weather will soon mildew and be no use for jam. The fruit is the first and biggest part of making jam. Next comes the syrup the fruit will sit in, and this needs much care.
passage.part_3: In the candy maker's art, it is very important to measure the strength of the syrup exactly for each case. They know this by signs, and express it by certain technical terms. But to tell these apart properly requires very great attention and much practice. The main thing to know is that, as the syrup boils longer, its water will boil away, and it will become thicker. Great care must be taken in controlling the fire, so that the syrup does not boil over. Do not carry the boiling so far that the sugar burns. The candy maker judges the syrup by its signs.

items.prompt: What two problems does the writer say sugar causes when it is used to keep fruit?

tutor_only.confirm: Sugar is costly, and it destroys the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentences 'The cost of keeping them with sugar is a serious problem' and 'Sugar is also too strong for and destroys the slightly sour taste so wanted in many fruits' state both problems directly.
tutor_only.tell: Sugar costs a lot, so keeping fruit that way is a serious problem. Sugar is too strong and destroys the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits.
help: Sugar costs a lot, so keeping fruit that way is a serious problem.
Sugar is too strong and destroys the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits.
tutor_only.core_idea: Sugar costs a lot and it destroys the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits.
accept_ideas: the cost of sugar is a serious problem
sugar is expensive so keeping fruit that way costs too much
sugar destroys the slightly sour taste wanted in many fruits
sugar is too strong for the taste people want in fruit
unless a lot of sugar is used, success is very uncertain
not_required: that sugared fruit is mainly for dessert
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say sugar keeps fruit fresh and plump for several days.
if_they_say.ask: Which part of the passage says that, and does it talk about sugar?

items.prompt: Sugar destroys the sour taste; sweet fruit is 'meant for dessert.' What should jam taste like?

tutor_only.confirm: The fruit's own sour taste should survive — the syrup preserves the fruit, it does not sweeten it into a dessert.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The answer comes from the sentences 'The cost of keeping them with sugar is a serious problem; for, unless the sugar is used in large amounts, success is very uncertain' and 'Sugar is also too strong for and destroys the slightly sour taste so wanted in many fruits.' The first gives the cost and uncertainty; the second gives the taste damage.
tutor_only.tell: The writer says sugar destroys the sour taste and sweet fruit is for dessert. So jam should keep the fruit's sour taste.
help: The cost sentence says sugar is a serious problem. The taste sentence says sugar destroys a wanted flavour.
Connect the problem of cost with the problem of ruined taste.
tutor_only.core_idea: The fruit's own sour taste should survive; the syrup preserves it, not turns it into dessert.
accept_ideas: The fruit's sour taste should survive.
Jam should not taste like a sweet dessert.
The syrup should preserve the fruit, not sweeten it.
The fruit's own taste should come through.
not_required: A list of all preservation methods
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say jam should be as sweet as dessert.
if_they_say.ask: What does the writer say sugar does to the sour taste?

tutor_only.full_idea: The fruit's own sour taste should survive; the syrup preserves it, not turns it into dessert.

items.prompt: Wet fruit 'will soon mildew and be no use for jam.' When does the care have to start?

tutor_only.confirm: Before the fruit reaches the pan — a spoiled pick cannot be saved by careful boiling.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Part 2 says, 'Fruit gathered in wet or foggy weather will soon mildew and be no use for jam.'
tutor_only.tell: The mildew line comes before the syrup steps. It shows the care starts in the picking, before the fruit reaches the pan.
help: Think about what happens to fruit in wet or foggy weather.
Use the line about mildew and jam.
accept_ideas: Before the fruit is picked.
Before it reaches the pan.
At picking time, not at the boiling.
A spoiled pick cannot be saved by boiling.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the care starts when the syrup boils.
if_they_say.ask: Where does the mildew warning come in the passage?

tutor_only.full_idea: The care must start before the fruit is picked or reaches the pan; a spoiled pick cannot be saved later.

items.prompt: The writer says wet fruit is 'no use for jam.' What does that absolute phrase do to the risk?

tutor_only.confirm: Wet fruit is ruined for jam.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence 'Fruit gathered in wet or foggy weather will soon mildew and be no use for jam' says the fruit is no use at all, not merely less good.
tutor_only.tell: The phrase says 'no use,' not 'less good.' Wet fruit is ruined for jam.
help: Read the sentence about wet or foggy weather. Notice the words 'soon mildew' and 'no use.'
Think about how those words make the dry-weather rule feel more serious.
tutor_only.core_idea: The phrase 'no use' makes wet fruit ruined for jam.
accept_ideas: The fruit is ruined for jam.
Wet fruit spoils the jam.
The risk is total, not partial.
It is not merely less good; it is no use.
Wet fruit is a complete loss for jam.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the fruit is only a little worse.
if_they_say.ask: What does 'no use for jam' say about how bad the fruit is?

items.prompt: The opening argues why fruit must be kept. What does the last part add about the work?

tutor_only.confirm: It shows the keeping itself is skilled work, not only the reason to keep fruit.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The opening gives reasons fruit is valuable and sugar is costly. The last part turns to the work: 'as the syrup boils longer, its water will boil away' and 'the syrup does not boil over.'
tutor_only.tell: The opening gives the reasons. The last part shows that the keeping itself is skilled work.
help: The opening spends time on why fruit is valuable and why sugar is a problem.
The last part spends time on measuring syrup by signs and controlling the fire.
tutor_only.core_idea: The last part shows the keeping itself is skilled work, not only why fruit should be kept.
accept_ideas: It shows the work is skilled.
The last part is about the hard work of the syrup, not only why you keep fruit.
It adds judging syrup by signs and holding the fire.
It shows the difficulty, not only the reason.
not_required: naming both the syrup signs and the fire
quoting the technical terms for syrup
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the last part repeats the reasons.
if_they_say.ask: What skill does the last part add?
